subject: The benchmark: nothing simple predicts direction here either, and the required lift is 10x what any baseline delivers
body:
Second version tonight. The benchmark this project never ran, and what it says.

THE QUESTION NOBODY HAD ASKED. Every test in this campaign asked whether TUNGSTEN's score predicts.
None asked whether ANYTHING does. Those are different questions and only the second one tells you
whether to fix the system or the premise.

So I ran six standard baselines under the identical 2.5/1.5 bracket, on the same bars, with the same
maths. Ranked by mean R:

    reversal_5      +0.0254
    reversal_1      +0.0085
    TUNGSTEN        +0.0021
    random          -0.0010
    ma_cross        -0.0198
    momentum_20     -0.0229

Nothing clears the significance bar at any horizon. But the ordering is mirror-symmetric: mean
reversion positive, trend following equally negative, random sitting between them. That is structure
rather than noise.

And the uncomfortable part: TUNGSTEN's direction IS the ma_cross baseline. Its largest component is
EMA20-versus-EMA50 alignment across five timeframes, which is a multi-timeframe moving-average
crossover, and plain ma_cross is the second-worst row in its own benchmark. The system is built on
the losing side of the only structure the table shows.

THE NUMBER THAT FRAMES ALL OF IT. At a spread of 0.6 ATR with a 2.5/1.5 bracket, the win-rate lift
required just to break even is 15.0 percentage points. The best baseline delivers about 1.5. That is
not a near miss, it is an order of magnitude, and it applies to mean reversion as much as to this
system. reversal_5 also decays between halves of the sample: t of 1.22 in the older half, 0.28 in
the newer.

WHAT THAT MEANS. It is the efficient-data world, or close enough. No simple directional signal on
M5 USDJPY over this sample survives anything. The composite is not failing where simpler methods
succeed -- there is no demonstrated simple signal here for it to fail against. The binding
constraint is the FREQUENCY, not the component design.

That points at one lever, and it is a configuration change rather than a research programme: the
same 15-point hurdle at M5 falls to roughly 3.7 points at H4, purely through the cost ratio,
because spread as a fraction of the move shrinks with the square root of holding time.

TWO THINGS MY OWN CONTROLS CAUGHT TONIGHT.

The random baseline "cleared" the bar on the first run, which is impossible. A flat bar has a
zero-signed forward return, which never matches plus or minus one, so every flat bar counted as a
miss for every signal and dragged all hit rates a point below fifty. Fixed. The control row earned
its place on its first outing.

And in the split-half check, random passed the "same side in both halves" test on 2 of 3 horizons.
So that consistency criterion does not discriminate at this sample size, and any finding resting on
it is resting on nothing. Worth knowing, because I nearly leaned on it.

Separately I closed a gate I had opened by accident: the per-symbol export copy I added earlier
opens the export for READING in order to duplicate it, which made C6.1's "is anyone consuming this
record" check start passing. The writer copying its own output is not the learner reading it. Fixed;
the verdict is back to the honest split one.

37 of 45. Run 5 -- the first calibration on a fully corrected scorer -- is still running.
